lessons.title: Largest Rectangle In Histogram
lessons.objective: Solve Largest Rectangle in Histogram using a monotonic increasing stack — understanding why maintaining the invariant allows computing the maximum area at each pop in O(n).
concepts: Problem: largest rectangle that fits within histogram bars
Brute force: O(n²) — try every pair of bars as boundaries
Key insight: a bar limits the height of any rectangle it is part of
Monotonic increasing stack: pop when new bar is shorter
Area computation at pop: height = popped bar, width = current index - new stack top - 1
Sentinel value: append height 0 to force all pops at the end
Why width formula uses new stack top after pop
Connection to Trapping Rain Water as the complementary problem
lessons.explanation: Largest Rectangle in Histogram is one of the hardest problems in this module and a Blind 75 problem. Given an array of bar heights, find the area of the largest rectangle that fits entirely within the bars. Brute force: for every pair of left and right boundaries, find the minimum height between them and compute the area — O(n²) or O(n³). Monotonic increasing stack: maintain a stack of bar indices in increasing height order. When a new bar is shorter than the stack top, the stack top can no longer extend further right — its rectangle is bounded on the right by the current index. Pop the top, compute the rectangle height as the popped bar's height. Compute the width: if the stack is now empty, the rectangle extends from index 0 to current-1, so width = current index. If the stack is not empty, the new stack top is the nearest bar to the left that is shorter than the popped bar, so width = current - new_stack_top - 1. Append a 0 sentinel at the end to force all remaining bars to be popped and processed.
lessons.analogy: Largest Rectangle is like measuring the biggest floor plan that fits under a jagged ceiling profile. You walk from left to right with a measuring tape. When you encounter a drop in the ceiling, you realise that everything taller behind you cannot extend forward anymore. So you measure all the rectangles that are now blocked from extending, record their sizes, and continue. The monotonic stack is your list of 'still possibly extending' bars — each one is measured and removed the moment it is blocked.

code_example.explanation: The width formula has two cases depending on whether the stack is empty after popping. If empty, the popped bar's rectangle extends all the way from index 0 to i-1, so width = i. If not empty, the new stack top is the nearest shorter bar to the left, so the rectangle is bounded between new_stack_top+1 and i-1, giving width = i - new_stack_top - 1. Drawing this on paper before coding is essential — this formula is where most bugs occur.

common_mistakes: Forgetting the sentinel value 0 at the end — without it, bars remaining in the stack after the loop never get their areas computed; appending a 0 forces all bars to be popped and measured during the final iteration

Getting the width formula wrong when the stack is empty after a pop — an empty stack means the popped bar is the shortest bar seen so far, so its rectangle extends from index 0 to i-1, giving width = i not width = i - (-1) - 1; draw the example on paper to internalise the formula

Using >= instead of > in the pop condition — using >= ensures bars of equal height are also popped and measured, avoiding duplicate counting; with > equal-height bars would remain in the stack and produce incorrect widths

Bars remaining in stack after main loop never get measured. Sentinel 0 is shorter than all bars — forces all remaining bars to pop and be measured in the final iteration.

Mark end of array

coding_quest.title: Largest Rectangle In Histogram
coding_quest.problem_statement: Given histogram bar heights, find the largest rectangle area. Write O(n^2) brute force first, then O(n) monotonic increasing stack with sentinel 0. Trace [2,1,5,6,2,3].

wrong_approach_shown_first.explanation: Two common bugs: (1) no sentinel — bars remaining in stack never measured. (2) > instead of >= — equal-height bars not handled correctly.
wrong_approach_shown_first.naive_complexity: O(n) but wrong answers — misses remaining bars

hints.text: Append 0 to heights first. Use monotonic INCREASING stack. Pop when heights[stack.top] >= heights[i] (use >= not >). When popping: h=heights of popped bar. Width: stack empty → w=i; else w=i-stack.top-1.

heights=[...heights,0];const stack=[];let maxArea=0;for(let i=0;i<heights.length;i++){while(stack.length&&heights[stack[stack.length-1]]>=heights[i]){const h=heights[stack.pop()];const w=!stack.length?i:i-stack[stack.length-1]-1;maxArea=Math.max(maxArea,h*w);}stack.push(i);}return maxArea;

theory_mcq.question: Why does the lesson use a MONOTONIC INCREASING stack for Largest Rectangle in Histogram, in contrast to the monotonic DECREASING stack used for Next Greater Element and Daily Temperatures?
options: The choice between increasing and decreasing is arbitrary with no actual reason

The key insight is 'a bar limits the height of any rectangle it is part of' — by maintaining an INCREASING stack (popping when the CURRENT bar is SHORTER than the stack top), each popped bar represents the limiting (shortest) height for a rectangle whose width can now be precisely calculated, since we've just found both the bar that ends its potential rectangle on the right (current bar, shorter) and can determine the left boundary from what remains on the stack
Increasing stacks are always faster than decreasing stacks
This problem doesn't actually use a monotonic stack at all
theory_mcq.explanation: The lesson's stated key insight directly explains this: when a SHORTER bar arrives, every TALLER bar on the stack can no longer extend its rectangle rightward past this point — so each such taller bar's MAXIMUM possible rectangle area can now be finalized and computed, which is exactly why popping happens specifically when a SHORTER (height-limiting) bar is encountered, requiring the stack to track bars in increasing order.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the lesson append a sentinel value of 0 to the end of the heights array before processing?
options: The sentinel has no functional purpose; it's purely decorative

Without the sentinel, any bars still remaining on the stack at the natural END of the array would never get popped (and thus their potential rectangles would never be computed) — appending a height-0 sentinel guarantees that EVERY remaining bar on the stack will be popped (since 0 is shorter than any actual bar height), forcing the algorithm to correctly compute and consider every bar's maximum rectangle before the function returns
The sentinel changes the input array's actual histogram shape
The sentinel is required by JavaScript syntax for array operations
theory_mcq.explanation: This matches the lesson's explicit explanation: 'Sentinel value: append height 0 to force all pops at the end' — without this, bars remaining on the stack when the loop naturally ends would never trigger the pop-and-compute-area logic, potentially missing the true maximum if the largest rectangle involves one of those un-popped bars.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `largestRectangleArea([2,1,5,6,2,3])` per the lesson's own worked example, focusing on i=4 (height 2, with sentinel appended). Which bars get popped, and what areas are computed?
options: No bars are popped at i=4

Two bars are popped at i=4: first index 3 (height 6) with width=4-2-1=1 giving area=6, then index 2 (height 5) with width=4-1-1=2 giving area=10 — both popped because the current height (2) is less than both, with widths computed using the NEW stack top after each respective pop
Only index 3 is popped, with an area of 6
All bars are popped simultaneously with a single combined area calculation
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact trace: 'i=4 (h=2): 2<6 -> pop 3, h=6, top=2 -> w=4-2-1=1, area=6. 2<5 -> pop 2, h=5, top=1 -> w=4-1-1=2, area=10' — the while loop pops index 3 first (LIFO), computing width using the stack's new top (index 2) AFTER that pop, then continues popping index 2, computing width using the NEXT new top (index 1) after THAT pop.

logic_mcq.question: Why does the width formula use `i - stack[stack.length-1] - 1` (the NEW stack top AFTER popping) rather than the OLD stack top from before the pop?
options: Either the old or new top would give the identical width; this distinction doesn't matter

The just-popped bar's rectangle is bounded on the LEFT by whatever bar remains JUST BELOW it on the stack (after removal) — that REMAINING bar represents the nearest bar to the left that is SHORTER than the popped bar (since the stack maintains increasing order, everything below the popped bar must be shorter), correctly establishing the left boundary of the popped bar's maximal rectangle; the OLD top (the bar that was just removed) is no longer relevant to this calculation since it's the bar whose area is being computed, not a boundary
Using the old top would cause a syntax error
The formula doesn't actually use the stack top at all
logic_mcq.explanation: This is the precise reasoning behind the width formula: after popping the limiting (just-removed) bar, the bar now exposed at the new stack top is the nearest SHORTER bar to its left (guaranteed by the monotonic increasing invariant) — this defines exactly how far the popped bar's rectangle could extend leftward, while the current index i defines how far right it extends (up to, but not including, i, since the bar AT i is what triggered the pop by being too short).

logic_mcq.question: What is the maximum area found across the entire trace of `largestRectangleArea([2,1,5,6,2,3])`, and at which step is it achieved?
options: Maximum area is 6, found at i=4 when popping index 3

Maximum area is 10, found at i=4 when popping index 2 (height 5, width 2) — this remains the maximum through the rest of the trace, since the subsequent areas computed at the sentinel step (i=6: areas 3, 8, 6) are all smaller than 10
Maximum area is 8, found at the very end
Maximum area is 2, the smallest bar height in the array
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's final stated result: 'maxArea = 10' — this value is established at i=4 (height=5, width=4-1-1=2, area=10) and remains the maximum throughout the rest of the trace, since the sentinel-triggered pops at i=6 produce smaller areas (3, 8, and 6 respectively), none of which exceed 10.

syntax_mcq.question: In `const width = stack.length === 0 ? i : i - stack[stack.length - 1] - 1;`, why does the width calculation differ when the stack becomes EMPTY after a pop, compared to when elements remain?
options: There's no actual difference; both branches compute the same thing

If the stack is EMPTY after popping (meaning the just-popped bar was the SHORTEST bar seen so far, with nothing shorter to its left within the array), its rectangle can extend all the way back to index 0 — so width is simply `i` (the full span from the start up to but not including the current index); if elements REMAIN on the stack, the rectangle is bounded on the left by the new top, so the formula `i - stack[top] - 1` correctly excludes that boundary bar from the width
The empty-stack case always returns a width of 0
This ternary expression contains a bug and should always use the same formula
syntax_mcq.explanation: An empty stack after popping means there's no bar to the left that's shorter than the just-popped bar within the processed range — so its rectangle could theoretically span from index 0 all the way to (but not including) the current index i, giving width=i; when bars remain, the new top establishes a concrete left boundary, requiring the more complex `i - stack[top] - 1` formula to exclude that boundary position from the width count.

lessons.title: Stack And Queue Problem Thinking
lessons.objective: Given any new problem, identify within 60 seconds whether a stack, queue, or monotonic stack is the correct data structure — and which specific sub-pattern to apply.
concepts: Stack recognition signals: LIFO, nesting, undo, DFS, bracket matching
Queue recognition signals: FIFO, level order, BFS, scheduling
Monotonic stack signals: next greater/smaller, span, histogram area
Decision tree: stack vs queue vs deque vs monotonic stack
Common stack traps: processing order, empty-stack guard
Module 4 Blind 75 / NeetCode 150 problems mapped
Skills unlocked: Stacks and Queues
Bridge to Module 5: recursion and sorting use stacks implicitly
lessons.explanation: After this module you have three data structure tools: stack, queue, and monotonic stack. The recognition signals: Stack — the problem involves nesting, matching pairs, undo/redo, expression evaluation, or DFS traversal. The phrase 'most recently seen' or 'last encountered' is a stack signal. Queue — the problem involves processing in arrival order, level-by-level traversal, BFS, or scheduling. The phrase 'in order received' or 'level by level' is a queue signal. Monotonic stack — the problem asks for the next greater or smaller element, the span of consecutive elements satisfying a condition, or an area/water calculation involving bars. The phrase 'next greater', 'nearest smaller', 'span', or 'histogram' is a monotonic stack signal. The deque (double-ended queue) appears in sliding window maximum problems (Module 11) — keep it in mind as a data structure that supports O(1) at both ends.
lessons.analogy: Stack, queue, and monotonic stack are three differently shaped conveyor belts in a factory. The stack belt only lets you take from the most recently placed end. The queue belt only lets you take from the oldest end. The monotonic stack belt automatically removes items that no longer satisfy a property as new items arrive. The problem description tells you which belt the factory uses — your job is to read the description and recognise the belt immediately.

code_example.explanation: Seven of the nine problems listed are Blind 75. Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation (#150) uses a plain number stack. These three plus the four explicitly taught in this module complete the Blind 75 stack section.

common_mistakes: Not recognising that DFS can be implemented with either an explicit stack or recursion (implicit call stack) — both are equivalent; when interviewers ask for an iterative DFS solution, replace the recursive call stack with an explicit stack

Reaching for a stack on BFS problems or a queue on DFS problems — BFS always uses a queue (FIFO ensures level-by-level processing); DFS always uses a stack (LIFO ensures depth-first processing); confusing them produces wrong traversal orders

Not solving the Blind 75 problems from this module before moving to Module 5 — Module 5 covers recursion and sorting which build on stack concepts; the problems in this module are easier to internalise now than after recursion adds another layer of complexity
